facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest contrary evidence is that the ratio overstates steady-state leverage: all of the acquired debt is in the balance sheet but only one month of acquired earnings is in the last twelve months, and the issuer's own pro forma revenue for the nine months of 2026 is USD 1,169,676 thousand against USD 1,028,925 thousand reported, a difference of USD 140,751 thousand. No pro forma EBITDA is stated, and the acquired business reported a net loss for its first month, so how much earnings the extra revenue adds is not established. A full quarter of the acquired fleet in the next report, the final purchase accounting, or a further fall in legacy earnings would each move the view. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; calculation C15

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the view that owner behaviour is not the risk is the size of the repurchase authorization against liquidity: USD 492,355 thousand remains while cash was USD 390,844 thousand at 2026-09-30, and the issuer repurchased USD 90.0 million of shares in 2025 in the year it refinanced. The view would change if the proxy statement names a large holder or a controlling relationship, if the indenture permits distributions beyond the authorization, or if buybacks resume while Wilson integration costs and the Middle East cost increases persist. The strongest evidence against the concentration view is that Europe/Mediterranean produced USD 71,836 thousand of nine-month 2026 vessel operating profit, 31.04% of the total and up 49.79% on a year earlier, so the profit base is broadening away from West Africa. facts.label: T2D.9 - Risk-level drivers
facts.text: Sponsor / Governance Risk Level: Medium. The level is driven by cash returned to shareholders and debt-funded acquisitions, because these let value leave or leverage rise before creditors see earnings, which implies sensitivity of liquidity and refinancing to the pace of buybacks. Countervailing evidence is the absence of a sponsor, dividends or liability management, and cash-funded repurchases that slowed in 2026. Further analysis requires the proxy statement and the executed debt documents.

facts.text: - Leverage is low and coverage strong, but both worsened with the Wilson acquisition. Net debt over derived EBITDA rose from 0.14x at 2025-12-31 to 0.92x at 2026-09-30 and total debt over EBITDA to 1.69x because the acquisition used cash and added acquired loans while adding one month of earnings, and cash interest cover fell from 11.40x to 8.03x because the first coupons on the 2030 notes were paid in 2026 and EBITDA fell. Pro forma net debt including the acquisition for 2025-12-31 is not established. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation D01

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 74; calculation D02; calculation D03; calculation D04

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the view that the profile is weakening is that part of the margin fall is probably transitory: the nine-month 2026 result carries USD 14.4 million of acquisition costs and about USD 9.0 million of conflict-related crew, insurance and fuel cost, third-quarter EBITDA was only 3.11% below the same quarter a year earlier, free cash flow remains well above interest and the notes trade above principal. The view would turn positive if a full quarter of the acquired fleet adds earnings and the conflict costs fade, and negative if the 8.48% nine-month EBITDA decline continues, if West Africa keeps shrinking, or if the revolver covenant definitions prove tighter than derived leverage suggests. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation D03; calculation D07; calculation D10

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Tidewater's strongest support is a low-leverage balance sheet: net debt of 0.92x derived EBITDA and cash interest cover of 8.03x leave room before debt service is stressed, which lowers near-term default risk. Liquidity of USD 640,844 thousand against debt due through 2029 of USD 141,707 thousand means all maturities through 2029 can be paid from cash, and free cash flow of USD 270,068 thousand, 52.98% of EBITDA, funds drydocking internally. A footprint of five segments in over thirty countries, with no customer at 10% of revenue in 2025, limits the effect of a single-market shock, and the first large maturity is in 2030. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation D01; calculation D06; calculation D08

facts.text: The main weaknesses are margin and revenue durability. The EBITDA margin fell 3.93 percentage points in nine months, many contracts run a year or less so revenue reprices quickly in both directions, and 76.68% of principal falls due in 2030 so a weak earnings year then would meet the refinancing. facts.label: Company description
facts.text: Tidewater time-charters offshore support vessels to oil and gas, offshore construction and windfarm customers in over thirty countries through five geographic segments, and platform supply vessels produced 72.3% of FY2025 vessel revenue against 24.2% for anchor handling towing supply vessels. The fleet is more than two hundred vessels with an average age of 14.0 years since the 22 platform supply vessels of the Wilson Companies joined on 2026-08-31, up from 13.1 years at the end of 2025. Because revenue follows utilization and day rates on contracts that are often a year or less, the cash flow that services debt is visible only a few quarters ahead, and an older fleet needs recurring drydock spending that competes with debt service. facts.label: Ownership and group structure
facts.text: Tidewater is publicly held with no sponsor or controlling holder named in the supplied documents, so there is no sponsor support to count on and no fund-life exit pressure; owner behaviour is rated medium risk because repurchases, acquisitions funded from cash and assumed debt and an unused authorization let value leave or leverage rise ahead of creditors. Debt sits at three levels: senior unsecured notes issued by the parent and guaranteed by subsidiaries, a senior secured revolver that is undrawn, and subsidiary-level secured borrowings of USD 239,990 thousand principal, held against vessels or bank guarantees and including the acquired Brazilian loans, so the USD 650.0 million of notes is unsecured alongside secured claims on specific assets, with intercreditor ranking not established. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; calculation D11

facts.label: Revenue durability
facts.text: Revenue is cyclical, short-dated and linked to offshore oil and gas spending. FY2025 utilization fell to 76.1% from 79.0% while average day rates rose 6.1%, and in the nine months of 2026 utilization rose to 78.1% from 75.3% with day rates up 1.1%, so rate gains are small and volume is the swing factor. Customer concentration is moderate, with the five largest customers at 29.8% and the ten largest at 47.9% of FY2025 revenue, and a Mexican customer paid USD 54.0 million of overdue amounts in late 2025, so counterparty collection is a live risk; the credit consequence is that a utilization slump of a few points would hit revenue immediately because contracts can be ended on 90 days or less notice. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 74–75; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39

facts.label: Margin resilience
facts.text: Margins are exposed to operating leverage and cost inflation. The issuer states that a sizeable part of vessel operating and depreciation cost does not change with revenue, crew cost is 59.11% of vessel operating cost, and customers pay fuel while a vessel is on hire but the issuer pays it when idle or in drydock. The EBITDA margin fell to 36.89% in nine months from 40.82%, with Middle East war bonuses, insurance and fuel and acquisition costs as the stated drivers, so margin can be defended only if day rates keep rising faster than crew and conflict cost, and the third-quarter margin of 34.69% was below the nine-month 36.89%, so pressure had not eased by September even though third-quarter EBITDA was only 3.11% below a year earlier against 8.48% for the nine months. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 30–31; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation D02; calculation D03; calculation D05

facts.label: Free cash flow conversion
facts.text: Free cash flow after drydock and tax is positive and well covered, but conversion depends on cycles the issuer does not control. Last-twelve-months operating cash flow of USD 314,403 thousand less additions to properties and equipment of USD 44,335 thousand left USD 270,068 thousand, 52.98% of EBITDA, after USD 101,751 thousand of drydock cash that EBITDA adds back through amortization, and tax charges were 63.83% of pre-tax income in the nine months, so conversion would fall if drydock timing bunches or tax burden stays high. Capex is modest and discretionary beyond drydocking, which gives flexibility, while acquisition integration cost and the payments on finance leases of USD 24,903 thousand in the nine months of 2026 consumed cash. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation D08; calculation D09

facts.label: Industry forces
facts.text: Rivalry is broad, with many competitors of all sizes, and competes on vessel suitability, availability and price, so day rates follow the supply of vessels against offshore spending. Buyers are large oil and gas companies and national oil companies on short contracts, which gives them power at renewal, while crew labour supplies the largest cost and local rules on content and ownership protect some markets such as US Gulf trade and raise cost in others. Substitutes are limited for offshore logistics, and windfarm support offers a partial alternative market; new entrants face high vessel cost but local-content rules can also exclude Tidewater from some contracts. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40

facts.label: Policy, currency and geopolitical factors
facts.text: Geopolitical and currency factors are material. The Iran conflict that began on 2026-02-28 raised crew, insurance and fuel cost at the Middle East segment, African customers pay locally so cash accumulates in currencies that are hard to repatriate, the Brazilian development bank loan terms require a domestic content percentage of at least 60%, and Pillar Two and US taxes lifted the tax charge. The economic factor is the oil price: the issuer says sustained prices in the low $60s per barrel may delay some drilling projects expected to start in 2026, which would weigh on day rates and utilization. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 73

facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: Scale and market position are strong: the group had revenue of USD 1,352,786 thousand in FY2025 and a fleet that grew with the acquisition, although the claim of the broadest operating footprint is management language. Competitive advantage is average because contracts are short and local-content rules help only in some markets. Business diversification is average: five segments and no customer at 10% of revenue in 2025, offset by 40.93% of segment profit in West Africa. Cost and capex flexibility is average, with crew cost at 59.11% of vessel operating cost and drydocking a recurring need but little discretionary capex. Margin stability is average and declining, free cash flow stability is average with USD 270,068 thousand of conversion, and the ability to refinance is average because the 2030 maturities are concentrated although the notes trade above principal. Liquidity is strong on stated figures, and financial policy and governance is average, with medium risk from repurchases and the acquisition. The trend is weaker margins and higher leverage after the acquisition, and the key missing data are covenant definitions, ratings and acquired earnings. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 101; calculation D01; calculation D02; calculation D05; calculation D07; calculation D08

facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer's own outlook is positive on offshore investment and energy security, but it also expects conflict-related costs to continue if the conflict does; tailwinds are higher European and Mediterranean day rates, a full quarter of the acquired fleet and no maturity of size before 2030, while headwinds are crew and insurance cost, integration cost, weaker West Africa activity and any project delays from low oil prices. Over three to five years the 2030 notes become callable at a premium from 2027-07-15 and at par from 2029-07-15, which opens a refinancing window ahead of the 2030 maturity if earnings hold. The credit consequence is that headroom is large today but depends on margins stabilising before the refinancing window opens. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The issuer-specific downside is a prolonged Middle East conflict and project delays from low oil prices that cut utilization and day rates in the Middle East and West Africa while crew, insurance and fuel cost stay high. Revenue and EBITDA fall because contracts reprice within a year, cash interest of USD 63,484 thousand, drydock cash of USD 101,751 thousand and acquisition integration cost do not fall with them, and the free cash flow of USD 270,068 thousand is 52.98% of EBITDA, so an EBITDA decline of that share with other items unchanged would remove it; cash and revolver of USD 640,844 thousand cover debt due through 2029 of USD 141,707 thousand 4.52 times on stated figures. Management levers are vessel sales, deferral of discretionary capex, suspending repurchases and drawing the revolver, so the scenario strains the refinancing of the 2030 notes more than liquidity, and the observable triggers are margin below the Q3 2026 level, a repurchase restart and any covenant waiver. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation D06; calculation D08; calculation D13

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Tidewater presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, geographic spread and a low-leverage balance sheet, but credit quality is constrained by falling margins, short contracts and a 2030 maturity concentration. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because free cash flow covers interest and drydocking, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on margins recovering before the call dates of the 2030 notes and on the integration of the Brazilian fleet. The primary downside path is a conflict- and oil-price-driven fall in utilization and day rates that outruns cost flexibility before the 2030 refinancing. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, ratings, acquired earnings and a numeric outlook. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: margin erosion in a short-contract, drydock-heavy fleet ahead of the 2030 refinancing. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation D01; calculation D02; calculation D06

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage on reported EBITDA is low but rose sharply: net debt reached 0.92x last-twelve-months EBITDA at 2026-09-30 against 0.14x at 2025-12-31, because the Wilson acquisition added debt and used cash while contributing one month of earnings.

### Key findings

Carrying-value debt rose from USD 654,893 thousand at 2025-12-31 to USD 862,260 thousand at 2026-09-30 while cash fell from USD 578,761 thousand to USD 390,844 thousand, so net debt rose from USD 76,132 thousand to USD 471,416 thousand. The Wilson acquisition accounts for the move: net cash paid for it was USD 272,975 thousand and the acquired loans stood at USD 224,506 thousand of principal at 2026-09-30, so it was funded from cash on hand and assumed loans, with no new borrowing in the nine months.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 100; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C10

Cash interest paid was USD 62,908 thousand in the nine months of 2026 against USD 47,234 thousand a year earlier, and reported EBITDA fell to USD 379,583 thousand from USD 414,770 thousand, a decline of 8.48%. The July 2025 refinancing left the senior notes due July 2030 paying one coupon each January and July, so two coupons fall inside the 2026 nine months and cash interest in any period is timing-sensitive.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation C03; calculation C11

Operating cash flow was USD 161,443 thousand in the nine months of 2026 against USD 226,148 thousand, and after additions to properties and equipment of USD 39,188 thousand free cash flow was USD 122,255 thousand against USD 205,534 thousand. The EBITDA used here adds back USD 84,118 thousand of drydock amortization while cash drydock spending was USD 87,898 thousand, so on the last-twelve-months basis net debt over EBITDA less cash drydock spending is 1.16x rather than 0.92x.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation C08; calculation C12

Cash of USD 390,844 thousand plus the undrawn USD 250.0 million revolver gives USD 640,844 thousand of stated liquidity at 2026-09-30, and about 21% of the cash held by foreign subsidiaries was awaiting conversion to dollars. Principal due through 2029 totals USD 141,707 thousand, while USD 682,474 thousand falls due in 2030, mostly the senior unsecured notes due July 2030, so refinancing pressure sits in 2030 rather than in the near term.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 43–44; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C08; calculation C13

The issuer prints no EBITDA and no total liabilities, so both are derived here, and the 2024 operating cash flow was revised upward by USD 8,623 thousand in the 2025 annual report; the revised figure is used throughout.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 100–104; 10-K_2024-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 105; calculation C03; calculation C07; calculation C14
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest contrary evidence is that the ratio overstates steady-state leverage: all of the acquired debt is in the balance sheet but only one month of acquired earnings is in the last twelve months, and the issuer's own pro forma revenue for the nine months of 2026 is USD 1,169,676 thousand against USD 1,028,925 thousand reported, a difference of USD 140,751 thousand. No pro forma EBITDA is stated, and the acquired business reported a net loss for its first month, so how much earnings the extra revenue adds is not established. A full quarter of the acquired fleet in the next report, the final purchase accounting, or a further fall in legacy earnings would each move the view.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; calculation C15
### Limitations

Reported EBITDA is derived as operating income plus depreciation and amortization and includes gains on asset dispositions, and the revolver covenant EBITDA is defined in an agreement that was not supplied, so covenant headroom is not established. Cash flows are printed only year to date, the 2025 interim reports as first filed were not supplied, and whether bank guarantees procured for the acquisition reduced revolver availability before 2026-10-02 is not stated, so undrawn capacity is the commitment less drawings only. Every ratio at 2026-09-30 uses principal and carrying values that include the acquired loans.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 26

## Gaps

- Earnings before depreciation and amortization, interest and tax is not stated by the issuer in any of the five documents, so EBITDA is derived as operating income plus depreciation and amortization for every period; this restricts every leverage and cover ratio to a derived measure, severity Medium, and the action is to obtain the covenant definition from the revolving credit agreement.
- No adjusted EBITDA or add-back list is stated, so the adjusted ratios and the EBITDA bridge are not supplied; severity Low, and the action is none unless the issuer publishes one.

- Loss on early extinguishment of debt is printed as a dash for FY2024, the nine months and the third quarter of 2026; the dash cells in the cash flow statement for proceeds from sale of notes, acquisitions, issuance of long-term debt, finance lease payments and the debt extinguishment premium, and the restricted cash line on the balance sheet, are likewise carried as not supplied rather than zero; severity Low, and the action is none.

- Wilson Companies results are in the statements from 2026-08-31 only, and their purchase accounting is provisional; the last-twelve-months ratios therefore mix all acquired debt with one month of acquired earnings, severity High, and the action is to refresh with the next quarterly report and the final purchase accounting.

- No pro forma net debt for 2025-12-31 including the acquisition is stated, so the Post-balance-sheet adjustments row for the acquisition carries no figure; severity Medium, and the action is to use the 2026-09-30 row.

- Whether the termination cost of the replacement guarantees was paid after 2026-09-30 is not stated, so the net debt effect of that event is not established; severity Low, and the action is to read the next quarterly report.

- Undrawn revolver capacity is the commitment less drawings; whether guarantees or letters of credit reduced availability at 2026-09-30 is not stated; severity Medium, and the action is to obtain the credit agreement and the closing report.

- Cash flows are printed only year to date, so quarterly cash flow figures and the fourth quarter of 2025 cash flow are not supplied and the third quarter of 2026 is not derived here; severity Low, and the action is to derive them from the year-to-date figures if needed.

- The 2025 interim reports as first filed were not supplied, so the revision of the 2025 interim cash flows cannot be tested and the nine-month 2025 operating cash flow is taken as printed in the 2026 report; severity Low, and the action is to obtain them if nine-month comparisons matter.

- The denomination of the acquired Brazilian loans and the yearly amortization of each loan are not stated, so the instrument register carries those cells as not supplied; severity Low, and the action is to read the loan agreements.

- Legal ranking among the secured borrowings is not stated; the debt stack groups them at one rank and names this limitation; severity Medium, and the action is to obtain the intercreditor and security documents.

- The sources are page text, so layout and footnote marks were read as text and not checked visually against the original filings; severity Low, and the action is to check key figures against the filings before committee use.

Scope: business model, ownership and control, governance and owner behaviour, operating model, issuer history and the Wilson acquisition of 2026-08-31, from the five supplied filings.
## Sources

No external sources were used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

Tidewater is a publicly held operator with no sponsor or controlling holder identified in the supplied documents, so creditor risk comes from earnings concentration in a short-contract vessel business and from the Wilson acquisition, not from owner behaviour.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40; Source readiness (CP-0)

West Africa produced 40.93% of segment vessel operating profit in FY2025 on 27.09% of vessel revenue, and many contracts run a year or less with termination on 90 days or less notice. The Wilson acquisition on 2026-08-31 added 22 vessels in Brazil and USD 224,506 thousand of loans, USD 189,678 thousand of which the parent guarantees.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 141–142; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C06

The unused USD 492,355 thousand of the share repurchase authorization is the main route for value to leave creditors, and the proxy statement and executed debt documents were not supplied, so shareholder control and legal capacity are not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 52; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

- Revenue visibility is short, so cash flow follows utilization and day rates quickly. Many contracts run a year or less and can be ended on 90 days or less notice, no backlog amount is stated, and nine-month 2026 utilization was 78.1% against 75.3% with an average day rate of USD 23,007 against USD 22,753, while vessel operating cost per active day rose 8.70% to USD 9,694.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation C09

- Earnings are concentrated in West Africa, which produced 40.93% of FY2025 segment vessel operating profit on 27.09% of vessel revenue. Its nine-month 2026 operating profit then fell 20.17% as the segment ran 55 vessels against 68 and day rates fell 10.4%, and about 21% of cash held by foreign subsidiaries was awaiting conversion to dollars, so local-currency receipts delay the cash that reaches the parent.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 141–142; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 42–43; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 44; calculation C02; calculation C04

- Customer concentration is moderate. The five largest customers were 29.8% and the ten largest 47.9% of FY2025 revenue, no customer reached 10% in 2025 against 12.3% for one customer in 2024, and a Mexican customer that paid USD 54.0 million of overdue amounts in the fourth quarter of 2025 still owed USD 12.4 million at 2025-12-31.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 86

- Operating cost shocks and uninsured idle time weigh on cash flow. Drydock costs are deferred and amortized over 30 months, cash drydock spending was USD 87,898 thousand in the nine months of 2026, the Iran conflict added about USD 5.4 million of crew and travel cost, USD 1.8 million of insurance and USD 1.8 million of fuel in the Middle East from March 2026, and the issuer does not generally buy business interruption insurance.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 31

- The Wilson acquisition changes the credit profile more than any owner behaviour. The issuer paid USD 283.1 million in cash against a base price of USD 500.0 million, assumed USD 229,047 thousand of debt at face, and now guarantees the BNDES construction loans and the Banco do Brasil loan, so a default on those loans could trigger cross-default into the 2030 notes and the revolver, and the purchase accounting is provisional.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 15–18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 51–52; calculation C05

- Capital returns are the owner behaviour that matters to creditors. About USD 215.7 million of shares were bought back over three years, USD 90.0 million in 2025 and USD 7.9 million in the nine months of 2026, funded from cash, no dividends were declared, and USD 492,355 thousand of the August 2025 authorization remained at 2026-09-30.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 46; calculation C07

- History shows debt-funded growth followed by refinancing, not distributions. The 2023 purchase of 37 vessels from Solstad cost about USD 594.2 million and was funded by cash, a term loan and notes, and in July 2025 the issuer replaced three instruments with USD 650.0 million of senior unsecured notes due 2030, paying redemption premiums of USD 15.0 million and USD 4.5 million.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 7
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the view that owner behaviour is not the risk is the size of the repurchase authorization against liquidity: USD 492,355 thousand remains while cash was USD 390,844 thousand at 2026-09-30, and the issuer repurchased USD 90.0 million of shares in 2025 in the year it refinanced. The view would change if the proxy statement names a large holder or a controlling relationship, if the indenture permits distributions beyond the authorization, or if buybacks resume while Wilson integration costs and the Middle East cost increases persist. The strongest evidence against the concentration view is that Europe/Mediterranean produced USD 71,836 thousand of nine-month 2026 vessel operating profit, 31.04% of the total and up 49.79% on a year earlier, so the profit base is broadening away from West Africa.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 40–42; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C07
### Limitations

- The proxy statement, which holds ownership, board and related-party detail, was not supplied, so the conclusion that no controlling holder exists rests on none being named in the annual report and would change if a large holder is named.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 145–147; Source readiness (CP-0)

- No indenture, credit agreement or BNDES loan agreement was supplied, so legal capacity for shareholder payments, new debt, liens and asset transfers is not established and the buyback conclusion describes an authorization, not a permitted amount.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14

- The Wilson Companies are in the statements for one month and their purchase accounting is provisional, so conclusions about the acquired earnings and the leverage effect of the acquisition are provisional until a full quarter and the final accounting are reported.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 7–9

- No investor presentation, earnings release, backlog figure or management outlook with numbers was supplied, so the revenue-visibility conclusion rests on contract terms in the risk factors and not on contracted days.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The Wilson acquisition is the one transaction that changes the creditor position in the period. Completed on 2026-08-31 under an amended and restated purchase agreement dated 2026-08-25, it bought all the capital stock of two Brazilian companies owning 22 platform supply vessels from three sellers, for a base price of USD 500.0 million reduced by the acquired companies' net debt and adjusted for working capital, which left USD 283.1 million paid in cash. The consideration was cash plus assumed loans, with no equity issued to the sellers.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 50; calculation C05

No new debt was issued in the nine months of 2026: the debt table adds USD 224,506 thousand of acquired BNDES and Banco do Brasil loans that the issuer assumed, the parent signed a guarantee agreement on 2026-09-21 that replaced the former guarantors of the BNDES construction loans from 2026-10-01, and the revolving credit facility was undrawn when the report was signed. The USD 650.0 million of senior unsecured notes due 2030 and the revolver were issued and signed on 2025-07-07, so they are not new in the period.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 43; calculation C06

The purchase accounting is provisional and open for up to a year, and the issuer expects to leave the acquired companies out of its internal-control assessment at 2026-12-31, so figures for the acquired business may change.

spans.text: ## Request

Tidewater Inc (issuer tdw-98222), fundamental credit synthesis as of 2026-11-18 under the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope: business and financial profile, liquidity and refinancing, financial policy, downside path and monitoring triggers, built from the five supplied filings and the accepted Source readiness, Financial foundation and Business & governance analyses.
## Sources

No external sources were used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

Tidewater's fundamental credit profile is solid but weakening: leverage is low and liquidity strong, yet margins are falling in a short-contract, drydock-heavy business, so creditors are exposed mainly to earnings erosion ahead of the 2030 refinancing and to the newly acquired Brazilian fleet.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation D01; calculation D02

Net debt was 0.92x last-twelve-months EBITDA at 2026-09-30 and cash interest cover 8.03x, with USD 640,844 thousand of cash and undrawn revolver, but the nine-month 2026 EBITDA margin fell to 36.89% from 40.82% and USD 682,474 thousand of principal falls due in 2030. The parent replaced the former owners as guarantor of the Brazilian construction loans on 2026-10-01 and the replacement bank guarantees ended on 2026-10-02, and any effect on net debt or revolver availability is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation D01; calculation D02; calculation D06
Covenant headroom, ratings and legal capacity are not established because no executed debt document or rating was supplied.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

- Leverage is low and coverage strong, but both worsened with the Wilson acquisition. Net debt over derived EBITDA rose from 0.14x at 2025-12-31 to 0.92x at 2026-09-30 and total debt over EBITDA to 1.69x because the acquisition used cash and added acquired loans while adding one month of earnings, and cash interest cover fell from 11.40x to 8.03x because the first coupons on the 2030 notes were paid in 2026 and EBITDA fell. Pro forma net debt including the acquisition for 2025-12-31 is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation D01

- Margins are the weakest dimension. The nine-month 2026 EBITDA margin was 36.89% against 40.82% a year earlier, a fall of 3.93 percentage points, as general and administrative cost rose 17.39% on acquisition costs and vessel operating cost per active day rose 8.70%, and crew cost is 59.11% of vessel operating cost, so wage premiums and conflict-related cost move straight into margin while revenue is repriced only as contracts renew.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 74; calculation D02; calculation D03; calculation D04

- Liquidity is strong on stated figures but untested. Cash of USD 390,844 thousand and the undrawn USD 250.0 million revolver give USD 640,844 thousand, cash covers current debt maturities 6.66x and debt due through 2029 2.76x, but covenant definitions and any reduction of revolver availability by guarantees are not established, and about 21% of cash held by foreign subsidiaries was awaiting conversion to dollars.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 43–44; calculation D06

- Refinancing risk sits in 2030. USD 682,474 thousand, 76.68% of principal, falls due in 2030, mostly the senior unsecured notes due July 2030, which can be called from 2027-07-15 at a premium that falls to par in 2029; the notes' fair value was 105.20% of principal at 2026-09-30, which points to market access, but ratings and quotes were not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation D06; calculation D07; Source readiness (CP-0)

- Cash conversion is good but carries recurring claims. Last-twelve-months free cash flow was USD 270,068 thousand, 52.98% of EBITDA, after drydock cash of USD 101,751 thousand and cash interest, and the nine-month 2026 tax charge was 63.83% of pre-tax income, so conversion is sensitive to tax and drydock cycles.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation D08; calculation D09

- Earnings are concentrated and the owner is a source of leakage risk, not support. West Africa produced 40.93% of FY2025 segment profit and its nine-month 2026 profit fell 20.17%, the ten largest customers were 47.9% of FY2025 revenue, and USD 492,355 thousand of the share repurchase authorization is unused with no sponsor to provide support.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 52; calculation D12

- The Wilson acquisition adds scale but concentrates integration and guarantee risk. The parent guarantees USD 189,678 thousand of the USD 224,506 thousand of acquired loans, having replaced the former owners as guarantor on 2026-10-01; a default on them could trigger cross-default into the notes and revolver, and the purchase accounting is provisional.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 51–52; calculation D11
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the view that the profile is weakening is that part of the margin fall is probably transitory: the nine-month 2026 result carries USD 14.4 million of acquisition costs and about USD 9.0 million of conflict-related crew, insurance and fuel cost, third-quarter EBITDA was only 3.11% below the same quarter a year earlier, free cash flow remains well above interest and the notes trade above principal. The view would turn positive if a full quarter of the acquired fleet adds earnings and the conflict costs fade, and negative if the 8.48% nine-month EBITDA decline continues, if West Africa keeps shrinking, or if the revolver covenant definitions prove tighter than derived leverage suggests.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation D03; calculation D07; calculation D10
### Limitations

- Covenant headroom is not calculable because the revolver tests net interest-bearing debt to EBITDA of 3 to 1 on definitions in an agreement that was not supplied, so the strong-leverage conclusion rests on a derived measure and would weaken if the contractual measure is stricter.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 14; Source readiness (CP-0)

- No rating, bond price or peer data was supplied, so the refinancing assessment rests on the maturity profile and the fair value of the notes and would change if a rating or quote shows a different market view.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13

- The outlook rests on management statements and one oil price remark, with no backlog amount or numeric guidance stated, so the 12 to 24 month view of utilization and day rates is a judgement that a disclosed contract backlog or a broker forecast could move.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 73
- Acquired earnings are not separately stated, so the post-acquisition leverage path and the downside scenario use the combined fleet without a standalone view of the Brazilian business.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9
### Strengths and weaknesses

Tidewater's strongest support is a low-leverage balance sheet: net debt of 0.92x derived EBITDA and cash interest cover of 8.03x leave room before debt service is stressed, which lowers near-term default risk. Liquidity of USD 640,844 thousand against debt due through 2029 of USD 141,707 thousand means all maturities through 2029 can be paid from cash, and free cash flow of USD 270,068 thousand, 52.98% of EBITDA, funds drydocking internally. A footprint of five segments in over thirty countries, with no customer at 10% of revenue in 2025, limits the effect of a single-market shock, and the first large maturity is in 2030.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation D01; calculation D06; calculation D08

The main weaknesses are margin and revenue durability. The EBITDA margin fell 3.93 percentage points in nine months, many contracts run a year or less so revenue reprices quickly in both directions, and 76.68% of principal falls due in 2030 so a weak earnings year then would meet the refinancing. West Africa produced 40.93% of FY2025 segment profit and then weakened, so one region sets much of the cash flow, and the Wilson acquisition brings integration cost, parent guarantees of USD 189,678 thousand and provisional accounting, while legal documents that would show distribution and debt capacity were not supplied.
Basis: calculation D02; calculation D06; calculation D11; calculation D12; Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

### Company description

Tidewater time-charters offshore support vessels to oil and gas, offshore construction and windfarm customers in over thirty countries through five geographic segments, and platform supply vessels produced 72.3% of FY2025 vessel revenue against 24.2% for anchor handling towing supply vessels. The fleet is more than two hundred vessels with an average age of 14.0 years since the 22 platform supply vessels of the Wilson Companies joined on 2026-08-31, up from 13.1 years at the end of 2025. Because revenue follows utilization and day rates on contracts that are often a year or less, the cash flow that services debt is visible only a few quarters ahead, and an older fleet needs recurring drydock spending that competes with debt service.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–6; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 70; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 30; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Ownership and group structure

Tidewater is publicly held with no sponsor or controlling holder named in the supplied documents, so there is no sponsor support to count on and no fund-life exit pressure; owner behaviour is rated medium risk because repurchases, acquisitions funded from cash and assumed debt and an unused authorization let value leave or leverage rise ahead of creditors. Debt sits at three levels: senior unsecured notes issued by the parent and guaranteed by subsidiaries, a senior secured revolver that is undrawn, and subsidiary-level secured borrowings of USD 239,990 thousand principal, held against vessels or bank guarantees and including the acquired Brazilian loans, so the USD 650.0 million of notes is unsecured alongside secured claims on specific assets, with intercreditor ranking not established.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; calculation D11
### Revenue durability

Revenue is cyclical, short-dated and linked to offshore oil and gas spending. FY2025 utilization fell to 76.1% from 79.0% while average day rates rose 6.1%, and in the nine months of 2026 utilization rose to 78.1% from 75.3% with day rates up 1.1%, so rate gains are small and volume is the swing factor. Customer concentration is moderate, with the five largest customers at 29.8% and the ten largest at 47.9% of FY2025 revenue, and a Mexican customer paid USD 54.0 million of overdue amounts in late 2025, so counterparty collection is a live risk; the credit consequence is that a utilization slump of a few points would hit revenue immediately because contracts can be ended on 90 days or less notice.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 74–75; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39
### Margin resilience

Margins are exposed to operating leverage and cost inflation. The issuer states that a sizeable part of vessel operating and depreciation cost does not change with revenue, crew cost is 59.11% of vessel operating cost, and customers pay fuel while a vessel is on hire but the issuer pays it when idle or in drydock. The EBITDA margin fell to 36.89% in nine months from 40.82%, with Middle East war bonuses, insurance and fuel and acquisition costs as the stated drivers, so margin can be defended only if day rates keep rising faster than crew and conflict cost, and the third-quarter margin of 34.69% was below the nine-month 36.89%, so pressure had not eased by September even though third-quarter EBITDA was only 3.11% below a year earlier against 8.48% for the nine months.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 30–31; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation D02; calculation D03; calculation D05
### Free cash flow conversion

Free cash flow after drydock and tax is positive and well covered, but conversion depends on cycles the issuer does not control. Last-twelve-months operating cash flow of USD 314,403 thousand less additions to properties and equipment of USD 44,335 thousand left USD 270,068 thousand, 52.98% of EBITDA, after USD 101,751 thousand of drydock cash that EBITDA adds back through amortization, and tax charges were 63.83% of pre-tax income in the nine months, so conversion would fall if drydock timing bunches or tax burden stays high. Capex is modest and discretionary beyond drydocking, which gives flexibility, while acquisition integration cost and the payments on finance leases of USD 24,903 thousand in the nine months of 2026 consumed cash.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation D08; calculation D09
### Industry forces

Rivalry is broad, with many competitors of all sizes, and competes on vessel suitability, availability and price, so day rates follow the supply of vessels against offshore spending. Buyers are large oil and gas companies and national oil companies on short contracts, which gives them power at renewal, while crew labour supplies the largest cost and local rules on content and ownership protect some markets such as US Gulf trade and raise cost in others. Substitutes are limited for offshore logistics, and windfarm support offers a partial alternative market; new entrants face high vessel cost but local-content rules can also exclude Tidewater from some contracts.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 40
### Policy, currency and geopolitical factors

Geopolitical and currency factors are material. The Iran conflict that began on 2026-02-28 raised crew, insurance and fuel cost at the Middle East segment, African customers pay locally so cash accumulates in currencies that are hard to repatriate, the Brazilian development bank loan terms require a domestic content percentage of at least 60%, and Pillar Two and US taxes lifted the tax charge. The economic factor is the oil price: the issuer says sustained prices in the low $60s per barrel may delay some drilling projects expected to start in 2026, which would weigh on day rates and utilization.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 73
### Credit-translated SWOT

- Strengths: low derived leverage of 0.92x net debt to EBITDA, cash interest cover of 8.03x, stated liquidity of USD 640,844 thousand, free cash flow of USD 270,068 thousand and no maturity of size before 2030.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation D01; calculation D08
- Weaknesses: falling margin, short contracts, 76.68% of principal due in 2030, profit concentration in West Africa and a parent exposed to USD 189,678 thousand of acquired-loan guarantees.
Basis: calculation D02; calculation D06; calculation D11; calculation D12

- Opportunities: a full quarter of the acquired Brazilian fleet could add earnings, European and Mediterranean profit grew 49.79% in nine months, and the unrecorded Venezuela judgment of about USD 87.0 million is an upside the issuer does not count.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 21
- Threats: continued conflict cost, an oil price in the low $60s per barrel that delays projects, integration problems and cross-default through the parent guarantees.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 51–52; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 73
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are strong: the group had revenue of USD 1,352,786 thousand in FY2025 and a fleet that grew with the acquisition, although the claim of the broadest operating footprint is management language. Competitive advantage is average because contracts are short and local-content rules help only in some markets. Business diversification is average: five segments and no customer at 10% of revenue in 2025, offset by 40.93% of segment profit in West Africa. Cost and capex flexibility is average, with crew cost at 59.11% of vessel operating cost and drydocking a recurring need but little discretionary capex. Margin stability is average and declining, free cash flow stability is average with USD 270,068 thousand of conversion, and the ability to refinance is average because the 2030 maturities are concentrated although the notes trade above principal. Liquidity is strong on stated figures, and financial policy and governance is average, with medium risk from repurchases and the acquisition. The trend is weaker margins and higher leverage after the acquisition, and the key missing data are covenant definitions, ratings and acquired earnings.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 101; calculation D01; calculation D02; calculation D05; calculation D07; calculation D08
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer's own outlook is positive on offshore investment and energy security, but it also expects conflict-related costs to continue if the conflict does; tailwinds are higher European and Mediterranean day rates, a full quarter of the acquired fleet and no maturity of size before 2030, while headwinds are crew and insurance cost, integration cost, weaker West Africa activity and any project delays from low oil prices. Over three to five years the 2030 notes become callable at a premium from 2027-07-15 and at par from 2029-07-15, which opens a refinancing window ahead of the 2030 maturity if earnings hold. The credit consequence is that headroom is large today but depends on margins stabilising before the refinancing window opens.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, pages 32–33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 73; calculation D06
### Downside scenario

The issuer-specific downside is a prolonged Middle East conflict and project delays from low oil prices that cut utilization and day rates in the Middle East and West Africa while crew, insurance and fuel cost stay high. Revenue and EBITDA fall because contracts reprice within a year, cash interest of USD 63,484 thousand, drydock cash of USD 101,751 thousand and acquisition integration cost do not fall with them, and the free cash flow of USD 270,068 thousand is 52.98% of EBITDA, so an EBITDA decline of that share with other items unchanged would remove it; cash and revolver of USD 640,844 thousand cover debt due through 2029 of USD 141,707 thousand 4.52 times on stated figures. Management levers are vessel sales, deferral of discretionary capex, suspending repurchases and drawing the revolver, so the scenario strains the refinancing of the 2030 notes more than liquidity, and the observable triggers are margin below the Q3 2026 level, a repurchase restart and any covenant waiver.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tdw.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation D06; calculation D08; calculation D13
### Overall credit view

Overall, Tidewater presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, geographic spread and a low-leverage balance sheet, but credit quality is constrained by falling margins, short contracts and a 2030 maturity concentration. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because free cash flow covers interest and drydocking, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on margins recovering before the call dates of the 2030 notes and on the integration of the Brazilian fleet. The primary downside path is a conflict- and oil-price-driven fall in utilization and day rates that outruns cost flexibility before the 2030 refinancing. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, ratings, acquired earnings and a numeric outlook. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: margin erosion in a short-contract, drydock-heavy fleet ahead of the 2030 refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation D01; calculation D02; calculation D06
